findings.title: Google credential overwritten with the zod SafeParse result object
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the full `safeParse` result (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed data. Before this change `key` was `googleCredentialSchema.parse(...)`, i.e. the token object. Now `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })` stores `{ success: true, data: {...} }` as the credential key. On the next load, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` fails, so every Google Calendar credential breaks after its first token refresh.

findings.title: `prisma` used without being imported
findings.body: The new code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)`, but this file never imports `@calcom/prisma`. This either fails type-check or throws a ReferenceError at runtime, so the Salesforce integration cannot be constructed at all.

findings.title: Salesforce refreshes the token on every instantiation and then ignores the new token
findings.body: `getClient` now POSTs to the Salesforce token endpoint every time the service is constructed, whether or not the token is expired. That adds latency and rate-limit pressure to every booking. The new `access_token` is written to the DB, but the returned `jsforce.Connection` is still built from the old `credentialKey.access_token`/`instance_url`. The refresh also bypasses `refreshOAuthTokens`, so sync mode never applies here. Separately, `response.statusText !== "OK"` is a fragile success check: statusText is empty over HTTP/2. Use `response.ok` instead.

findings.title: Minimum token schema uses bogus computed keys and strips expiry fields
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal key "[object Object]". The second one overwrites the first. The resulting schema is effectively `{ access_token, "[object Object]"?: unknown }`, and `z.object` strips all unknown keys. In sync mode every refreshed response therefore loses its expiry field (`expires_in`/`expiry_date`/etc.). For example, Zoom computes `expiry_date` from `undefined` and gets NaN, and Office365 stores no expiry. Tokens are then treated as perpetually expired or invalid. Use `.passthrough()` or an explicit schema.

findings.title: Placeholder refresh_token overwrites the real refresh token
findings.body: When the provider response has no `refresh_token`, the helper sets it to the literal string "refresh_token". This also runs when syncing is disabled. Office365 spreads `tokenResponse.data` over the stored credentials, so a refresh response without a refresh_token replaces the user's real refresh token with "refresh_token". All future refreshes then fail. Google also receives this value via `googleCredentials`. The placeholder should only apply in sync mode, and should not clobber an existing stored token.

findings.title: Sync path returns a fetch Response while callers expect SDK/axios result shapes
findings.body:
In sync mode the helper returns a raw `fetch` Response. Several callers expect a different shape:
- Google reads `res?.data` (a gaxios response).
- Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin read `tokenInfo.data` (axios).
- HubSpot expects a `HubspotToken` object.

With a Response, `.data` is undefined, so Google/Zoho throw on `token.access_token` or `tokenInfo.data.error`. HubSpot stores a Response object as the credential key with NaN `expiryDate`. The sync feature is broken for these apps. Normalize to parsed JSON, or have each caller handle both shapes.

findings.title: Outgoing credential-sync request carries no authentication
findings.body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug`, with no shared secret or signature. The self-hoster's endpoint, which returns live third-party access tokens, cannot verify that the caller is Cal.com. Anyone who can reach it can enumerate user IDs and harvest tokens. Include the webhook secret header or an HMAC signature.

findings.title: Credential ID passed where user ID is expected
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes the credential id as the third argument, which is `userId`. In sync mode the self-hosted endpoint is asked for tokens of an unrelated user whose id happens to equal the credential id. This can attach another user's tokens to this credential. It also forces the sync path even for team credentials. Pass `credential.userId`.

findings.title: Wrong app slug "zoomvideo" sent to the sync endpoint
findings.body: The Zoom app's slug/appId is "zoom" (see `createOAuthAppCredential({ appId: "zoom", ... })`). The refresh call sends `appSlug: "zoomvideo"`, which differs from the slug the webhook endpoint uses. A self-hoster's sync endpoint keyed by app slug won't recognize it.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared non-constant-time; malformed input yields 500s
findings.body:
The secret header is compared with `!==`, which is vulnerable to timing attacks; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. Also:
- There is no HTTP method check.
- `schema.parse` throws on a bad body.
- `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throws on a bad ciphertext or key.

All of these surface as unhandled 500s instead of 400s on an endpoint that writes credentials.
